summary: A brick light of 1865 at the tip of Stonington Peninsula, automated in 1922 and put out in 1936; the tower still stands in a Hiawatha National Forest picnic area.

light.characteristic: Fl W 30s until 1922, then one-second flash every ten seconds

lens.where: Taken out of the lantern in 1922 when the light was automated (Terry Pepper); the sources read do not say where it went

access.note: Forest Service site. The last mile of road is single-lane, narrow and winding; the Forest Service advises against RVs and trailers over 16 ft long or 8 ft high.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS record says 'Demolished by Usfs' and the station record notes a source saying the structure is gone. The Forest Service, Terry Pepper and LighthouseFriends all describe the brick tower standing; what was demolished or removed was the keeper's dwelling after its 1959 fire.

LighthouseFriends dates the transfer to 1 November 1936; Terry Pepper and the Forest Service date the Forest Service's custodianship to 1937. The record can carry the 1936 transfer with the 1937 custody noted.
The 'Fl W 30s' in the record is the character from 1865 to 1922. Both LighthouseFriends and Terry Pepper record the 1922 change to a one-second flash every ten seconds.

corrections.why: The 30-second character belongs to 1865-1922. Both sources record the change in 1922 to one-second flashes every ten seconds (Terry Pepper: a one-second flash followed by a nine-second eclipse).

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-22: story corrected against the cached sources. Changed: the payroll line (it shows first appearance, not the opening date); Terry Pepper's ownership transfer in 1937 (the story had said custody); the ice winter (Terry Pepper 1887-88, LighthouseFriends 1885-86, now stated as a disagreement); the lightship's sale (Terry Pepper: the year after its 1925 removal); the road (the Forest Service says the last 0.8 mile); the monarch wording (a 'popular spot to enjoy'); the NRHP date (NPGallery publication date); units added. Checked: the Board 1894 lightship passage starts on printed p. 147 and runs onto p. 148 (cited p. 147 is right); Johnson's Point Peninsula line falls under the sundry civil act approved 2 March 1889 (scan p. 33). Corgan: the Bulletin 1924 notice OCR reads 'Henry Oorgan'; the Bulletin 1912-17 and 1924-29 indexes both read 'Corgan, Henry', so the name is confirmed by print, not only by position. No page image was rendered (the cached Bulletin is text only). Tower height:the USLHS record gives 36 ft (tower) and 41 ft (focal height); Terry Pepper, LighthouseFriends and the Forest Service give about 40 ft; the station record has 11.0 m. The story uses 40 ft. First lighting: Terry Pepper's payroll evidence points to autumn 1865; Rowlett's directory (cited in the station record) and some other lists give 1866. Not checked against a primary source here. Armstrong's last year: USLHS and LighthouseFriends's Escanaba appointment point to 1922; Terry Pepper says 1925. The 1864 act: Terry Pepper gives 20 July on one page and 2 July on another; LighthouseFriends gives 2 July. The NRHP nomination (75000941) is a not-digitized placeholder on NPGallery, so the nomination text was not read. Lens: Terry Pepper's first page says Argand lamps and reflectors in the lantern; its second page and LighthouseFriends say the fourth-order Fresnel lens was there from 1865. The Bulletin's OCR prints Corgan as 'Oorgan'; the name is matched to the USLHS roster as 'Henry Corgan' by the Bulletin's station list (Point Peninsula). Johnson's 1889 appropriation line is OCR'd with errors; only the station name and 'two thousand dollars' are quoted. The 1936 transfer date and the 1925 departure are both disputed (see resolved_conflicts). Mid-1890s wrecks in the logbook come only through LighthouseFriends's transcription of a 1949 pioneer-day display: check the original logbook if one is found. A Chronicling America search for the Lucie Graham wreck (1913, Michigan papers) returned no hits.
